concepts.description: Static product pages show a product, but a real-time conversation resolves the buyer's specific situation at the moment of decision.
High-intent buyers leave a product page when it cannot answer 'is this right for MY situation', returning to search or competitors.
Evidence of 25-60% and up to 4x conversion gains when product pages can answer specific questions in real time.
Reframing lost sales as a conversation the page cannot have, rather than a traffic or content problem.
AI makes early exploration nearly free, letting a PM try many product versions before committing to one.
The scarce resource is the judgment call about which version of the product is worth building next, not iteration speed.
Every iteration is a different answer to what the product actually does, not merely an added feature.
Running two models side by side to expose limitations instead of hiding them, building user trust.
Positioning a product version against the gap an incumbent ignores, such as investigation versus storage.
A strong average score can conceal catastrophic errors in exactly the cases where being right matters most.
Building evals from clustered real user feedback and the scenarios that matter, not from the data you happen to have.
Scoring AI failures on severity, harm scope, immediacy, and reversibility to distinguish bug classes.
Detecting scene dynamics first, then changing sampling rate, prompts, and review defaults for high-motion footage.
Publicly demonstrating an AI product's failure mode instead of only its working demo.
PM owns the experience, engineer owns the implementation, and the working prototype bridges the two.
Converting a validated AI-built prototype into a complete English spec that engineers re-implement without ambiguity.
The PM validates the most expensive discovery risk in a prototype before it hits the engineering queue.
The most efficient shipping unit is an engineer with great product taste, so PM and engineering roles converge.
The real cost question is deciding where intelligence is needed at all, not making inference cheaper.
Optical flow, a motion threshold, then a cheap model process only the 10% of footage that matters, cutting cost 10x.
Keith Rabois's distinction between people who drive decisions end-to-end and people who execute handed tasks.

concepts.concept: Most footage should not reach AI
concepts.description: Pre-filtering with near-zero-cost methods so the majority of input never incurs model cost.
When anyone can ship a working prototype in an afternoon, opinion-based design decisions become the differentiator.
Tony Fadell's term for accepting AI output without questioning it, losing the informed gut that produces taste.
Details like staged loading animations and visible hashes exist to create trust and feeling, not function.
Taste built by running the product and noticing what feels off, rather than following a spec.
The AI never guesses negotiated terms; it structures and fills known values and asks when data is missing.
Colleagues adopted the system precisely because it is predictable and unexciting rather than impressive.
Breaking a workflow apart by which parts require human judgment and which are fill-in-the-blank.
A feedback loop that converts reviewer notes into permanent system rules.
Extracting calibration baselines from dozens of real signed agreements to validate generated drafts.
Generation is dangerous for structured documents; filling tokens into a fixed template is reliable, auditable, repeatable.
Replacing every variable field with a unique token so legal boilerplate, numbering, and formatting are never touched.
Word splits a sentence across formatting runs, so naive find-and-replace silently corrupts documents.
Separating what goes into a document from what it looks like as the basis of reliable document automation.
Word documents carry comments and tracked changes separately; reading only one layer misses the real review.
Never overwrite the reviewer's marked-up copy; save it before building the next clean version.
Human review is an interface you design, assuming feedback lives in more places than the obvious one, not a checkpoint phase.
A review checkpoint only works if the system knows how to read and preserve what came back.
High agency is not a personality trait but a system you decide to build.
One source of product intent rendered as a prototype for business, a spec for engineers, and a policy framing for legal.
One document read differently by every team, with the mismatch surfacing weeks later when builds diverge.
Presenting the system that produced the work rather than a portfolio of outputs.
The real gap between failed and successful AI builds is whether iteration converges to done, not speed.
A tangled single-file build that no second person, or even the author, can safely change.
Separated modules, version control, and design docs make an AI build something a team can inherit and grow.
Once convergence holds, an AI workflow stops being one person's productivity and becomes a team's work pattern.
The scarce skill is building systems that transform public signals into a positioning judgment, not information retrieval.
An industry CPTO independently corroborating market reads the system produced months earlier from public data.
Starting an interview or product process with a market thesis rather than a build.
Building first-party models only where differentiation, cost, or latency demand it, using general LLMs elsewhere.
Knowing how much confidence to place in a system-produced judgment is part of the skill.
Sorting each idea by whether the market discusses it and whether you have covered it: covered, open, and owned territory.
Ideas you keep advancing that few others discuss are your potential differentiation to protect.

concepts.concept: Blind spot from inside the feed
concepts.description: Embedding comparison surfaced a safety coverage gap invisible from within one's own content.

concepts.concept: Sorting is compute, call is judgment
concepts.description: Similarity scores are computation; deciding which gap is worth entering remains human judgment.
Luhmann's principle that ideas become useful when placed in relation to other ideas, applied to writing in public.
